it Contents 15px Sans Snug Relaxed Airy Ch. 1 — Chapter I — I Set Off Upon My Journey To The House Of Shaws DEDICATION MY DEAR CHARLES BAXTER: If you ever read this tale, you will likely ask yourself more questions than I should care to answer: as for instance how the Appin murder has come to fall in the year 1751, how the Torran rocks have crept so near to Earraid, or why the printed trial is silent as to all that touches David Balfour. These are nuts beyond my ability to crack. But if you tried me on the point of Alan’s guilt or innocence, I think I could defend the reading of the text. To this day you will find the tradition of Appin clear in Alan’s favour. If you inquire, you may even hear that the descendants of “the other man” who fired the shot are in the country to this day. But that other man’s name, inquire as you please, you shall not hear; for the Highlander values a secret for itself and for the congenial exercise of keeping it. I might go on for long to justify one point and own another indefensible; it is more honest to confess at once how little I am touched by the desire of accuracy. This is no furniture for the scholar’s library, but a book for the winter evening school-room when the tasks are over and the hour for bed draws near; and honest Alan, who was a grim old fire-eater in his day has in this new avatar no more desperate purpose than to steal some young gentleman’s attention from his Ovid, carry him awhile into the Highlands and the last century, and pack him to bed with some engaging images to mingle with his dreams. As for you, my dear Charles, I do not even ask you to like this tale. But perhaps when he is older, your son will; he may then be pleased to find his father’s name on the fly-leaf; and in the meanwhile it pleases me to set it there, in memory of many days that were happy and some (now perhaps as pleasant to remember) that were sad. If it is strange for me to look back from a distance both in time and space on these bygone adventures of our youth, it must be stranger for you who tread the same streets--who may to-morrow open the door of the old Speculative, where we begin to rank with Scott and Robert Emmet and the beloved and inglorious Macbean--or may

David reaches the neglected estate and calls through a barred door to its unseen master. 3 scenes · 2,449 words Read to here Ch. 2 — Chapter II — I Come To My Journey’s End — Neighbours describe Shaws and its solitary owner before David approaches the tower. Ebenezer questions the stranger outside while keeping bolts and walls between them. The letter forces Ebenezer to acknowledge his nephew and offer grudging shelter. 3 scenes · 1,942 words Read to here Ch. 3 — Chapter III — I Make Acquaintance Of My Uncle — David studies his uncle’s meanness while Ebenezer probes what the boy knows. Questions about David’s father expose fear beneath Ebenezer’s hostility. From his sparse chamber, David weighs Ebenezer’s promise of information and money against the danger gathering in the house. 3 scenes · 2,670 words Read to here Ch. 4 — Chapter IV — I Run A Great Danger In The House Of Shaws — David climbs the unfinished tower stair without lamp or warning. Wind and lightning reveal a fatal gap at the head of the stair just before David falls. David returns alive, forces Ebenezer to yield, and demands movement toward a lawyer. 3 scenes · 2,984 words Read to here Ch. 5 — Chapter V — I Go To The Queen’s Ferry — Ebenezer conducts David to the Forth while trying to recover control of their bargain. A bruised cabin-boy brings Captain Hoseason’s invitation from the Covenant. Ebenezer and Hoseason confer while David learns that Rankeillor knows the Balfour family. 3 scenes · 2,410 words Read to here Ch. 6 — Chapter VI — What Befell At The Queen’s Ferry — Hoseason coaxes David into visiting the brig before the tide changes.
